-This page is Worktrunk's **code signing policy**. It describes what gets signed, which certificate is used, how the signing pipeline works, and who authorizes each release. It exists both to document the process for users and to satisfy the transparency requirements of the [SignPath Foundation](https://signpath.org/) open-source code signing program.
+Worktrunk's SignPath Foundation application is under review. The Windows signing pipeline currently uses a self-signed test certificate and allows unsigned releases if signing fails.
 
 ## Why signing matters
 
-Worktrunk's Windows binaries (`wt.exe` and `git-wt.exe`) are small, native executables. Microsoft Defender's machine-learning heuristics routinely flag unsigned native executables of this shape as generic threats (for example `Trojan:Win32/Wacatac.B!ml`) — a false positive driven by the *absence of a trusted signature*, not by anything in the code. A valid [Authenticode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/install/authenticode) signature gives Defender's cloud something signed to trust, which is what stops that class of false positive. Signing the Windows artifacts is the durable fix.
-
-The macOS and Linux release artifacts, the crates.io source distribution, and `cargo install` builds are unaffected by this policy — `cargo install` compiles locally from source and never downloads a pre-built artifact.
+[Authenticode](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/install/authenticode) signatures identify a binary's publisher and verify that it has not changed since signing.
 
 ## Signing certificate
 
 > Free code signing provided by [SignPath.io](https://signpath.io/), certificate by [SignPath Foundation](https://signpath.org/).
 
-The certificate's private key is generated and held on SignPath's Hardware Security Module (HSM); no maintainer ever possesses the private key. Signing happens only through SignPath's service, invoked from Worktrunk's release pipeline.
+SignPath holds the private key in a hardware security module; maintainers do not have access to it.
 
 ## What is signed
 
-- `wt.exe` and `git-wt.exe` — the Windows binaries shipped in the `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` release archive on each [GitHub Release](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/releases) and distributed via [winget](https://github.com/microsoft/winget-pkgs) (`winget install max-sixty.worktrunk`). `git-wt.exe` is the same program built as a git subcommand.
-
-Nothing else is signed under this policy. Signed artifacts contain only code built from this repository; any bundled third-party libraries are used unmodified.
+The signing pipeline covers `wt.exe` and `git-wt.exe` in the `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` archive on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/releases), also distributed through winget.
 
 ## Build and signing pipeline
 
-1. Every release is triggered by pushing a version tag to [`max-sixty/worktrunk`](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk). No release is built from any other source.
-2. The [`release` workflow](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yaml) builds the platform binaries with [cargo-dist](https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/) on GitHub-hosted runners, from the tagged commit only.
-3. The Windows binary is submitted to SignPath for signing via the [SignPath GitHub Action](https://github.com/SignPath/github-action-submit-signing-request). The signed binary is returned to the workflow and published in the release archive.
-4. The build is reproducible from public source: the workflow, the toolchain pin ([`rust-toolchain.toml`](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/main/rust-toolchain.toml)), and the release configuration ([`dist-workspace.toml`](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/main/dist-workspace.toml)) are all tracked in this repository.
+The [`release` workflow](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yaml) builds tagged commits with [cargo-dist](https://axodotdev.github.io/cargo-dist/) on GitHub-hosted runners. It submits the Windows archive to SignPath and publishes the signed archive when signing succeeds.
 
 ## Project roles
 
-Worktrunk follows SignPath's team model:
+[@max-sixty](https://github.com/max-sixty) holds all signing roles:
 
-| Role | Responsibility | Who |
-|------|----------------|-----|
-| **Author** | Trusted developer who commits and tags releases | [@max-sixty](https://github.com/max-sixty) |
-| **Reviewer** | Reviews contributions from outside the trusted set before they can be released | [@max-sixty](https://github.com/max-sixty) |
-| **Approver** | Authorizes each signing request for a release | [@max-sixty](https://github.com/max-sixty) |
+- **Author**: commits code and tags releases.
+- **Reviewer**: reviews external contributions before release.
+- **Approver**: authorizes signing requests.
 
-All maintainers with signing authority use multi-factor authentication on their GitHub and SignPath accounts.
+Maintainers with signing authority use multi-factor authentication on GitHub and SignPath.
 
 ## Release approval
 
-Every signing request requires **manual approval** by an Approver before the certificate is applied — signing is never fully automated. A release is signed only after the Approver has confirmed the artifact was built from the tagged commit in this repository.
+Under this policy, each signing request requires manual approval after confirming that the artifact was built from the repository's tagged commit.
 
 ## Privacy
 
-Worktrunk is a local-first command-line tool. It performs no telemetry, collects no analytics, and transmits no user data. Network access happens only when a command the user ran needs it (for example, fetching CI status for `wt list --full`); the [FAQ](/faq/) and inline documentation describe exactly when. The signed binaries add no data collection of any kind.
+Worktrunk collects no telemetry or analytics. It transfers information to other systems only for operations requested or configured by the user.
 
 ## Reporting a problem
 
-If you believe a signed Worktrunk binary has been tampered with, or you receive an antivirus detection on an official release artifact, please [open an issue](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/issues). For a suspected Defender false positive, you can also report the file to Microsoft through the [Windows Defender submission portal](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/filesubmission) (as *"I believe this file is safe"*), which corrects the cloud definition for every user.
+Report suspected tampering or antivirus detections on official release artifacts by [opening an issue](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/issues). Suspected Defender false positives can also be submitted to [Microsoft for review](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/wdsi/filesubmission).

title: Clear repeated Git config values completely
body:
`git config --unset` returns status 5 both when a key is absent and when it has multiple values. Worktrunk treats that status as absence, so clearing repeated state values can report success while leaving the values on disk and removing them only from the in-memory cache.

Use `--unset-all` in the shared key-clearing helper. Status 5 then means absence, and a successful clear removes every value for the selected key. Add coverage for cached and fresh reads, repeated clears, and both named-variable and `--all` CLI paths.

Unreadable system and user config files are silently ignored, allowing commands such as `switch --create` to proceed with defaults. Missing-file behavior and layer precedence stay the same.

The shared path removes 25 lines of duplicated loading logic. Update the save-failure prompt test to make the path unwritable after the prompt appears, using the existing callback; it now isolates a save failure from a startup read failure.

title: Propagate failed Git predicates instead of treating them as missing refs
body:
When a ref query fails, `wt switch --create` can treat the branch as absent and create it from a fallback base. The same predicate helper can cache a failed `merge-base --is-ancestor` (for example, a missing object) as a permanent `false`.

Give `run_command_check` Git's predicate contract: status 0 is true, 1 is false, and anything else propagates the command error. `ref_exists` uses quiet `rev-parse --verify`, which follows that contract, and `exists_locally` reuses it. Switch base selection and the pre-add branch check propagate failures instead of defaulting to "absent". `wt list` now reports a failed ancestry query alongside its other failed tasks (one snapshot updated).

Tests: a switch regression where a failing `rev-parse` must stop creation, and a unit test that a failed ancestry query is not cached.

title: Test same-basename trash staging without depending on drain timing

The same-basename prune regression assumes each removal creates a separate background-drain log. The removal path intentionally reuses a running drain, so the assertion depends on scheduling and can fail when both worktrees were correctly staged and removed.

Move this invariant to the staging boundary: stage two registered worktrees with the same basename, verify that each keeps its registration-derived destination, and verify that both staged directories survive distinctly. Existing integration tests retain command-level prune coverage. No production removal behavior changes.

title: feat(remove): back up uncommitted changes before `--force` discards them
body:
`wt remove --force` now saves a worktree's uncommitted changes before discarding them, using the same `refs/wt-backup/<branch>` ref and reflog that the squash backup in `wt merge` / `wt step squash` already uses. The output then prints the backup and a recovery command:

```
▲ Discarding uncommitted changes (--force):
  ?? devbox.lock
↳ Backup created @ refs/wt-backup/feature-untracked (690353c)
↳ To recover in a new worktree, run wt switch --create --base 690353c… --no-hooks recovery/690353c
```

Closes #4544.

## What gets saved

- Staged, unstaged, and untracked files go into the snapshot, which is what `git add -A` would stage. The snapshot is built through a `TempIndex`, so the real index and the stash list are left alone.
- Ignored files, such as build output, are not saved. For submodules, only the checked-out commit is recorded; uncommitted changes inside a submodule are not saved.
- The backup commit's parent is the worktree's `HEAD`, so the branch tip also stays reachable after `-D` deletes the branch. On an unborn branch the commit has no parent.
- The backup is taken only when `--force` actually discards something. A clean `--force` removal creates no ref.

## Decisions for review

- **Always on, no flag.** This follows the issue thread: a flag would grow the CLI, and always saving means `-f` loses nothing you can't get back.
- **A failed backup refuses the removal.** The error is `Failed to back up uncommitted changes; worktree not removed`, followed by git's own error, and the "Discarding uncommitted changes" warning is printed only after the backup succeeds. That follows the data-safety guidance in AGENTS.md. It means `wt remove -f` now refuses a worktree that `git add -A` can't snapshot, such as one holding an unreadable non-ignored file or an untracked nested repo with no commits. A worktree whose `git status` fails (for example, a corrupt index) still has no backup and is removed as before (#4347). The alternative is to warn and continue.
- **Cost.** Untracked files that aren't ignored are written as blobs. A large unignored artifact makes the removal slower and grows the object store until the reflog entry expires. Nothing prunes `refs/wt-backup/` today, and this PR doesn't change that.

## Code

`create_safety_backup` and the new `create_removal_backup` (`src/git/repository/working_tree.rs`) share a `record_backup` helper for the `commit-tree` / `update-ref` step. The helper looks up the branch name without the cache, and falls back to `symbolic-ref` so an unborn branch is still named. The removal side lives in `stage_worktree_removal` (`src/git/remove.rs`). That function runs right before the worktree is renamed into trash, so it covers `wt remove`, `wt merge --remove`, and the foreground path.

## Tests

- `test_remove_force_with_untracked_files` now checks that the backup ref holds the untracked file's content, that its parent is the removed branch tip, and that an ignored file is excluded.
- A new unit test covers the unbo

title: fix(switch): handle fork branch conflicts on GitLab and Azure DevOps
body:
`wt switch` now handles a fork PR or MR whose branch name is already used locally on GitLab and Azure DevOps, matching the existing GitHub and Gitea behavior. GitLab uses the source project's namespace as a prefix, including nested groups; Azure DevOps uses the fork repository name. The prefixed branch tracks the PR or MR ref and remains fetch-only, so it cannot push to the fork.

The change also updates the `wt switch` help and its generated documentation to describe the shared behavior. Integration tests cover GitLab conflicts with and without existing tracking, Azure DevOps conflicts, and the no-conflict Azure path. The prefixed-name unit tests, docs sync test, and help snapshots pass locally.

title: perf(commit): skip the second staging pass when no pre-commit hook ran
body:
When no pre-commit hook is configured, `wt step commit`, `wt step squash` and `wt merge` now stage once instead of twice. Before this change, each of them ran an extra untracked-file `git status` and `git add -A` for nothing. On a large repo, each of those is a full worktree scan.

#4520 made every commit path stage before and after the pre-commit hooks. The pass after the hooks exists so a formatter hook's edits land in the commit. It was gated on hooks being *enabled*, not on any hook *running*. `execute_hook` already returns whether a hook ran, so the second `auto_stage` now runs only then. When a hook does run, both passes happen as before.

The new `test_commit_stages_once_without_pre_commit_hook` covers `wt merge` and `wt step commit` with no hook configured. It counts the untracked-file scans in the `-vv` trace: one with this change, two without it. The existing #4520 tests cover the case where a hook runs and still pass.

Locally, the clippy, doc and doctest steps of the pre-merge gate passed. Seven tests failed with and without this change, so the sandbox causes them: it blocks Unix sockets (the non-regular-file and fsmonitor tests) and lacks PowerShell and commit signing.

title: fix(remove): derive the trash directory in `wt _drain-trash` instead of taking it as an argument
body:
The hidden `wt _drain-trash <dir>` deleted every `<name>-<digits>` entry in whatever directory it was given, with no prompt: `wt _drain-trash ~` would delete `~/backup-2024` and `~/proj-2` and leave a `~.lock` beside it. Worktrunk only ever passed `repo.wt_trash_dir()`, but nothing tied the argument to a trash directory. It now takes no argument and drains `<git-common-dir>/wt/trash` of the repository it discovers; outside a repository it fails and deletes nothing. Both spawn sites run it as `wt -C <git-common-dir> _drain-trash`, since a removal's spawn cwd can be the empty placeholder of the worktree it just removed (`wt remove -D` of a bare repository's primary worktree from inside it), which in a sibling layout is in no repository.

Discovering the repository in the child exposed a second problem: detached children inherited the parent's git discovery variables. Run as a `!wt` alias, `wt remove` of the current worktree inherits a `GIT_DIR` naming that worktree's gitdir, which the removal prunes, so the drain failed with "not a git repository" and the trash stayed. Background hook pipelines already failed the same way. `spawn_detached_exec` now scrubs inherited discovery variables, as every other child whose cwd `wt` chooses does (`scrub_git_discovery_env_vars`).

Tests: `test_drain_trash_derives_the_trash_from_the_repository` covers both the scratch-directory case (fails, deletes nothing) and a drain from `.git/wt`. `test_remove_drains_trash_under_inherited_git_dir` covers the alias case, and it fails without the scrub.

title: fix(signals): stop foreground loops when wt itself receives Ctrl-C
body:
## What regressed

Since v0.80.0, Ctrl-C during `wt remove a b c` no longer stops the batch when the pre-remove hook catches SIGINT and exits normally, as pre-commit does (`trap '...' INT; exit 130`). Reproduced with a hook that traps INT, exits 130 and otherwise sleeps, plus a process-group SIGINT: v0.80.0 stops at `a` and keeps every worktree; current main removes `b` and `c`, branches included, and runs their hooks. `wt step prune` did the same with a hook that exits 0 after catching the key: every candidate was removed and wt exited 0.

Two changes combined. #4400 moved foreground children into the caller's native job group and followed the shell's wait-and-cooperative-exit rule, so a child that handles the key keeps its own exit status. #4357 made a multi-target remove continue past a failing target.

## The rule

Max chose the batch-runner convention (make, ninja, cargo) over the shell's: Ctrl-C that wt itself receives stops the current command. The terminal delivers SIGINT to the whole foreground job, so wt receives the key alongside the child. A shell waits and exits only if the child died of the signal, because the child might be an interactive program using Ctrl-C as input. A batch runner's steps aren't interactive, and the user pressing Ctrl-C means "stop the batch". For a destructive loop like remove or prune, that rule is also the one the data-safety principle asks for.

The child still handles the key its own way, and wt never signals it for INT. Once the child exits, the command starts nothing more and exits interrupted (native SIGINT re-raise / 130), whatever status the child chose. Numeric exit codes such as 130 are still never read as cancellation; wt's own receipt is the evidence.

## What changes

- `src/signal_forwarder.rs`: the existing per-operation cancellation (`CommandOperation`) gains a SIGINT flag beside its SIGTERM one. Foreground scopes register it, so the scope reports cancellation when its child exits, and later admissions in the same command are refused. The output drain's fresh flag, which existed to ignore keys the children had already handled, is gone.
- Covered loops: hook pipelines (including Warn-strategy post-* hooks), multi-step aliases, `for-each`, multi-target `remove` and `prune`.
- A command's final interactive child keeps the key as input and its own exit status: help and `config show` pagers, `--execute` programs and custom `wt-*` subcommands opt in through `Cmd::hand_off_terminal` (`TerminalInterrupt::ChildInput`). So does an alias's last serial step (`ForegroundStdin::HandOff`), since the alias is the whole command; `agent = "claude"` keeps claude's status after the user stops a turn with Ctrl-C. Otherwise pressing Ctrl-C in `less`, a REPL started by `-x` or such an alias, then quitting normally, would turn into exit 130. Earlier alias steps, concurrent groups and every hook step still cancel.
- Unchanged: between children, idle SIGINT still kills wt natively. Detached background hooks, timeout-bou

title: fix(switch): refuse --path naming the bare repository; drop rm -rf hint for --path
body:
Two problems with the new `wt switch --path` flag from #4317, found in release review.

**Bare repository moved aside.** `wt switch --create x --path proj.git --clobber` in a bare clone with no worktrees printed `Moved ~/proj.git to ~/proj.git.bak.<ts> (--clobber)` and created a worktree in the repository's place. `reject_path_overlapping_worktrees` skipped a requested path equal to any entry it checks, which is right for a registered worktree (`validate_worktree_creation` reports it by branch) but nothing later checks the git common dir. The guard now refuses that case with `--path <dir> is the repository's git directory`. The template route has the same exposure and is left to #4461; this guard runs only for `--path`.

While there, the guard compares paths with `canonicalize_with_parents` rather than `dunce::canonicalize`, so a deep Windows path and the short root containing it get the same prefix spelling for `starts_with` (the #3898 mismatch).

**`rm -rf` hint for a user-named directory.** When the `--path` directory exists, the hint suggested `rm -rf <path>`, though `--path` can name any directory, such as a project. For `--path` it now reads `To place the worktree elsewhere, choose a different --path; to overwrite (with backup), run wt switch --create --clobber <branch> --path=<path>`. The template route's hint is unchanged.

**Verification:** reproduced both on a build of `main` and confirmed the fix on this branch. `test_bare_repo_switch_path_rejects_the_repository` fails with the old guard (its snapshot shows the `Moved … (--clobber)` line), and the `switch_path_occupied` snapshot shows the new hint. `test_switch_path_naming_another_worktree` pins that `--path` naming another branch's worktree, with `--clobber`, still reports that worktree's branch and leaves it in place. Ran the switch, bare-repository and error-display integration tests, clippy, and pre-commit.

title: test(remove): retry the drain when a forked child still holds the trash lock
body:
The nightly `feature-powerset` job [failed](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/actions/runs/39376521570) in `git::remove::tests::drain_trash_deletes_staged_entries_once_the_lock_is_free` (added in #4516) with `assertion failed: staged_trash_entries(&trash).is_empty()`. This is a race in the test, not a bug in the drain. After the test drops its lock holder, it expects the next `drain_trash` to get the lock. But another test in the same process can fork a child while the holder is open. That child inherits the descriptor, and the flock stays held until it execs. The drain sees `WouldBlock` and exits, leaving the deletion to the holder, as designed. `test_configure_shell_opens_rc_with_exclusive_lock` has the same race on the rc-file lock.

Both tests now wait for the release through the shared `testing::wait_for` helper. It polls with a bounded timeout and stops at the first success, so on Windows the test never asks a handle that already holds the lock to take it again.

Verification: I reproduced the race with a scratch test that ran the same lock/release/drain sequence 2000 times while four threads spawned `true` in a loop. The first drain left the entry behind in 17–20 of the 2000 iterations. With the retry, no iteration left it. Both tests pass locally, and clippy is clean.

The same window exists in production, but it only delays cleanup: a staged entry waits in the trash until the next removal's drain. The doc comment on `trash_drain_running` already accepts a similar window, so this PR doesn't change the drain itself.

Refs #4509

title: fix(state): keep a var named `marker` when clearing all markers
body:
`wt config state marker clear --all` deleted a user variable named `marker` along with the markers. A var `marker` is stored at `worktrunk.state.<branch>.vars.marker`, and the clear matched every key against `^worktrunk\.state\..+\.marker$`, so `wt config state vars set marker hello` followed by `marker clear --all` silently removed the var and reported it as a cleared marker. `wt config state clear --all` hit the same path. Vars are hand-authored state with no way to regenerate them.

The clear now skips a `.vars.marker` key unless its value is marker JSON (`{"marker": "..."}`). Git can't tell the two apart from the key alone: branch `topic.vars`'s marker has the same key shape as a var `marker` on branch `topic`. The value check is the same one `all_markers` (used by `marker list`) already applies, so `--all` clears what the listing shows as markers.

The new `test_state_clear_marker_all_keeps_var_named_marker` failed before the fix: it reported `Cleared 3 markers` instead of 2, and the var was gone. It passes now, along with the other `test_state_clear*` tests.

title: test(picker): wait for rendered rows before the escape-abort snapshot
body:
`test_switch_picker_abort_with_escape` failed on Windows in the `affected` run on main ([run 39373658313](https://github.com/max-sixty/worktrunk/actions/runs/39373658313)). Its list snapshot held only the prompt line `>`, with no header and no `@ main` row. The commit that triggered the run (#4516, trash draining) doesn't touch the picker, so this is a test timing race.

**Cause.** This is the only capture-before-abort test that passes no inputs (`&[]`). So the only thing that gates its capture is `boot_picker_pty`: it waits for the `> ` prompt, then for the screen to sit unchanged for `STABLE_DURATION` (500ms). Items load asynchronously. On a loaded Windows runner the prompt can stay quiet for 500ms before the first row arrives, and the test captures that frame.

**Fix.** Gate the capture on `"has no file changes"`. That preview text appears only after the list has a selected row, so it confirms both panels before the capture. The sibling tests already gate the same way (`&[("", Some("plain-branch"))]`, `&[("", Some("@ main"))]`). If the preview never renders, the test now panics after 30s and shows the screen, instead of producing a snapshot diff. The committed snapshots don't change.

**Verification.** All 32 `switch_picker` tests pass locally with `--features shell-integration-tests`. I couldn't reproduce the race on Linux, even under CPU load (0/15 runs on the original code), so the evidence is the code path above plus the failing frame from the run.

title: fix(config): keep approvals and [projects] entries saved under v0.80.0 identifiers
body:
Since v0.80.0, #4421 changed the project identifier for three kinds of remote: a non-default SSH port joins the host (`host:2222/o/r`, was `host/o/r`), hosts are lowercased (`github.com/o/r`, was `GitHub.com/o/r`), and `git+ssh://` / `ssh+git://` URLs parse (`github.com/o/r`, was the raw URL). Approvals and `[projects."…"]` settings saved under the old identifier silently stopped applying. A non-interactive `wt switch --create` then failed with "Cannot prompt for approval" for hooks the user had approved, and ignored the project's `worktree-path`.

`Repository::project_identifier` now returns a `ProjectId` that carries the current identifier plus, where it differs, the identifier v0.80.0 computed for the same remote. `legacy_project_identifier` in `src/git/url.rs` is a frozen copy of the pre-#4421 rule. It returns nothing for an `ssh://` IPv6 remote, whose v0.80.0 identifier (`[2001/o/r`) collided across distinct hosts.

`matching_keys`, the one matcher behind both approvals and `[projects]` settings, also matches keys against the legacy identifier and ranks them below every key matching the current one. Settings under a current key override legacy ones field by field. Approvals under either key apply, so approving a new command (saved under the current identifier) keeps the earlier approvals in force without any migration. The per-project `wt config approvals` operations (stale approvals in `list`, `clear`, `clear --stale`) treat the legacy exact key like the current one. Writes and the displayed identifier stay on the current identifier. Most of the diff is the read APIs switching from `&str` to `&ProjectId`.

For the port case this restores v0.80.0's sharing. The legacy key `host/o/r` is also the live key of the same project on port 22, so a repo on `host:2222` reads approvals and settings saved for the port-22 remote, including ones saved after upgrading, and clearing from it removes them. #4421 had separated those; telling old entries from new ones would need provenance in `approvals.toml`, which this PR doesn't add. Keys written under `host:2222/o/r` apply only to that remote.

Verification: I reproduced the regression with the v0.80.0 and main binaries for all three remote forms, using approvals and `worktree-path` keyed under the old identifier. On this branch, `wt switch --create` (stdin closed) runs the approved hook in the legacy `worktree-path` again, as on v0.80.0. New tests: an integration test running `wt switch --create` with a case per remote form, an updated identifier-selection test, and unit tests for the legacy derivation, ranking and clear. The integration tests fail when the legacy identifier is withheld. Lib and bin tests, the approval, config, hook, merge and prune integration tests, clippy, rustdoc and pre-commit pass.

title: fix(shell): keep the Nushell wrapper working when its stdout is redirected
body:
Since #4400 rewrote the Nushell wrapper around `try … finally`, redirecting the stdout of a `wt` command that prints nothing there aborts the wrapper. `nu --no-config-file -c 'source init.nu; cd repo; wt switch --create y o> /dev/null; print $env.PWD'` prints `repo.y` on v0.80.0, but on main it fails with `nu::shell::cant_convert ... can't convert nothing to string` at the `try {`, stops the script, and loses the cd.

Nushell 0.116 fails to convert a `try … finally` that evaluates to nothing under `o>` or `o+e>`. A plain `try`, `| ignore` and `e>` are unaffected. The wrapper's `try … finally` now evaluates to a record holding the exit code and captured stdout, and the wrapper returns stdout or propagates the failure after the block, as v0.80.0 did. A failure's stdout still prints inside the block, so a failing cd directive can't drop it, and the `finally` still applies the directive and removes the temp files on Ctrl-C. Returning `""` from the empty branch would also have avoided the error, but it prints a blank line when `wt switch` is the last command of a `nu -c` script.

Verified with nu 0.116.0 against v0.80.0, main and this branch: `o> /dev/null`, `o> file`, `| ignore`, `e> /dev/null`, `o+e> /dev/null`, plain and captured (`let x = (wt switch …)`) calls, a stdout-producing command redirected and piped, a failing command (exit 1 with no source trace, with and without `o>`), and `--execute` under `o>` all match v0.80.0 on this branch. Main fails the `o> /dev/null`, `o> file`, `o+e>` and `--execute` under `o>` cases. An interactive PTY session runs `wt switch` with and without `o> /dev/null` and changes directory both times. The new `test_nu_wrapper_redirected_stdout_applies_cd` fails on main with the same `cant_convert` error and passes here. The nushell, shell-wrapper, init and foreground-job integration tests (291) pass with `--features shell-integration-tests`.

title: fix(templates): add the tojson filter for structured vars
body:
Since the minijinja 3 upgrade in #4442, `{{ vars.cfg }}` renders a JSON object or array var in Python style (`{'port': 3000}`) where v0.80.0 rendered JSON, and `{{ vars.cfg | tojson }}` fails with "unknown filter" because minijinja's `json` feature was off. Since #3129 removed JSON on hook stdin, templates are how hooks get structured values, so they had no way to pass one to `jq` or `curl -d`.

This enables the `json` feature and documents `tojson` beside the vars dot-access example in `wt hook --help`. `tojson` writes `'`, `<`, `>` and `&` inside strings as `\u` escapes, which JSON parsers decode; the shell formatter still single-quotes the result, so `-d {{ vars.config | tojson }}` passes one argument.

Two adjustments come with the feature. It makes minijinja choose JSON autoescaping from a template name ending in `.json`, `.js`, `.yaml` or `.yml`, as it already did HTML escaping for `.html`. Worktrunk's template names are config keys, so a custom column named `json` would have rendered JSON-quoted cells, and one named `html` already rendered HTML-escaped cells; the shared template environment now turns name-based autoescaping off. minijinja's `tojson` also writes an undefined value as `null`, so a wrapper rejects it the way printing does, and a mistyped `vars` key errors instead of sending `null`.

Verified by rerunning the release-review repro against the branch binary: `{{ vars.cfg | tojson }}` now renders `{"list": [1, 2], "port": 3000}`, and a custom column named `json` or `html` renders the raw value. New coverage: a doc-template test for the documented `curl` example in POSIX mode, a missing-key `tojson` error case, and the custom-column test now uses a header named `json`. Each of the three fails with its part of the change reverted.

Bare `{{ vars.cfg }}` still renders Python-style; `tojson` is the supported way to get JSON.

title: fix(alias): report an alias child killed by a signal other than INT/TERM
body:
Since v0.80.0, an alias whose child dies by a signal other than SIGINT/SIGTERM (for example `crash = "kill -KILL $$"`, or a segfaulting program) exits 128+N with no output. v0.80.0 printed `✗ Killed by signal N`. #4352 and #4400 limited interrupt classification to SIGINT/SIGTERM, so these deaths now reach `alias_error_wrapper`, which turns every child exit code into a silent `AlreadyDisplayed`. wt exits normally rather than dying by the signal, so the shell reports nothing either.

`alias_error_wrapper` now maps a child exit with a physical signal to `WorktrunkError::Interrupted`, the variant custom subcommands (`wt-foo`) already use for the same case. It renders `Killed by signal N` and exits 128+N. SIGINT and SIGTERM still short-circuit earlier and are re-raised for the shell to report, as AGENTS.md "Signal Handling" specifies, so `kill -TERM $$` stays silent from wt. Hooks and `wt step for-each` already report the signal in their own failure lines and are unchanged.

Verified with the release-review repros: SEGV and KILL aliases print `✗ Killed by signal 11` / `9` and exit 139 / 137, matching v0.80.0, for single, multi-step and concurrent aliases; `exit 2` stays silent. The new unix-only `test_step_alias_killed_by_signal` snapshot fails without the fix.

title: fix(shell): skip the shell config scan when the install offer can't prompt
body:
Since v0.80.0, every `wt switch` without an active shell wrapper spawns `pwsh` when PowerShell is installed, adding about 150-200 ms per call. That includes non-interactive calls such as `wt switch -c x --format json` from agents. #4422 made the shell config scan ask the installed `pwsh` for its profile path, and `prompt_shell_integration` ran that scan before checking whether it could prompt. When it can't prompt (no TTY, `--execute`, or a previously declined offer), both outcomes of the scan print the same install hint.

The can't-prompt check now runs before the scan, so those calls spawn neither `pwsh` nor `nu`.

Verified with logging `pwsh`/`nu` shims on PATH and the `-vv` trace: a non-TTY `wt switch b1` and `wt switch -c x1 --format json` spawned `nu` and `pwsh` on main and neither on this branch, and printed the same hint. Under `script` (a TTY), the switch still runs both probes and shows the install prompt. `test_switch_hint_skips_shell_config_scan` asserts through mock call logs that neither probe runs, and fails without the fix. It replaces `test_switch_offer_after_powershell_query`, which tested cancelling the scan's `pwsh` query in a non-TTY switch, a query that no longer happens there. That cancellation coverage moves to a PTY test, `test_offer_stops_on_cancelled_powershell_query`: on a terminal, SIGINT or SIGTERM in the query stops the switch with no offer, and an ordinary exit 130 still falls back to the offer.

title: fix: resolve every no-argument default through `@`, which outside a worktree names HEAD's branch
body:
Since v0.80.0, `wt switch @` run outside any worktree treats the directory it runs in as a detached worktree. This happens from a bare repository's directory (or the `proj/` holding `proj/.git` → `.bare`) and from a normal repository's `.git` directory. It prints `Already on worktree for detached worktree @ <dir>`, runs pre-switch hooks with no branch, and cds into the directory. v0.80.0 switched to the worktree of the branch HEAD names.

#4496 routed `wt switch` arguments through `Repository::resolve_worktree`. Its `@` arm expected `current_worktree().root()` to fail outside a worktree, but `WorkingTree::root()` falls back to the cwd. `@` now resolves to the registered worktree at the cwd's root and, where none is registered, falls through to the branch HEAD names, as `expand_selector` already reads `@`. The unreachable `GitError::NotInWorktree` is removed.

## One definition of the current worktree

The no-argument forms of other commands read `current_worktree().root()` and `.branch()` directly, so "the current worktree" had a second definition, and outside every worktree the two disagreed: `wt remove` and `wt remove @` took different code paths and gave different answers. Every no-argument default is now `selector.unwrap_or("@")`, so each command has one path with or without an argument:

- `wt remove` with no argument goes through `validate_remove_targets` with `["@"]`. Its separate single-target path is gone, and so is the `@` guard an earlier commit on this branch added beside it.
- `CommandEnv::for_action` and `for_action_loading_config` are deleted. `wt merge`, `wt step commit`, `wt step squash` (including `--show-prompt` / `--dry-run`), `wt hook` and `wt hook show` use `CommandEnv::for_selector("@")`.
- `wt step diff` resolves `@` the way it resolves `--branch`.
- `wt step copy-ignored` defaults `--to` to `@`. Run from a bare repository's directory, it used to copy ignored files into the bare repository itself (in v0.80.0 too).
- `wt config state` and `wt step push --no-ff` use `require_selected_branch("@")`; `Repository::require_current_branch` is deleted.

Inside a worktree these commands behave as before. `Repository::rooted_at` keeps the invoking repository when the selected worktree is the one it was discovered in, and `@` matches the worktree by path, so detached worktrees and duplicate checkouts of one branch resolve to themselves. `require_selected_branch` no longer names the detached worktree the user is standing in: `wt config state vars set` there says `Cannot set variable: not on a branch (detached HEAD)` with a plain `git switch <branch>` hint.

## Behavior change outside a worktree

From a bare repository's directory or a `.git` directory, `wt remove`, `wt merge`, `wt step commit`, `wt step squash`, `wt step diff` and `wt hook` now act on the worktree of the branch HEAD names, where they used to treat the directory itself as a worktree. `wt config state … --branch @` and `--to @` act on HEAD's branch there too. title: fix(commit): stage before pre-commit hooks as well as after
body:
Since v0.80.0, pre-commit hooks during `wt merge` and `wt step squash` no longer see the uncommitted changes in the index. #4321 moved the squash path to run hooks before staging so a formatter hook's edits would land in the squash commit. A hook that reads the index (`pre-commit run`, lint-staged, `git diff --cached`) then saw nothing staged and passed, so a merge that v0.80.0 blocked committed the offending changes.

All commit paths now stage, run the pre-commit hooks, and stage again with the same `--stage` mode. Hooks see the changes, formatter edits still land in the commit, and the generated commit message reads the post-hook index. The second staging warns only about untracked paths the hooks created. This also applies to `wt step commit` and `wt merge --no-squash`, which ran hooks before staging even in v0.80.0, so an index-reading hook now blocks those commits too, and a failed hook leaves the changes staged there as it already did for squash.

Verified with the release-review repros: a `git diff --cached` gate and a pre-commit-framework `pre-commit run` gate both block `wt merge` and `wt step squash` again, as on v0.80.0, where main committed the changes. A `sed` formatter hook's edit is in the commit and in the prompt the commit-message command receives, with a clean tree afterwards. The new `test_pre_commit_hook_sees_staged_changes` covers `wt merge` and `wt step commit` and fails without the fix. `test_step_commit_refuses_hook_created_conflict` now unstages in its hook, because `git merge` refuses to start once the index is staged. The other snapshot changes move the auto-staging warning ahead of the hook output.

title: fix(shell_exec): write small command input to a pipe, not a temp file
body:
Since v0.80.0, an unusable `TMPDIR` broke every command that passes input to a child: background hooks never spawned ("Failed to prepare detached input"), `wt step for-each` failed, `wt list` lost the working-tree diff of a worktree with untracked files (`git add --pathspec-from-file=-` failed), and background `wt remove` exited 1 after already removing the worktree. #4400 moved this input from a pipe to an anonymous temp file, even when it was empty.

The temp file exists so that no writer thread can block on a child that doesn't read its input. A pipe meets that requirement when the whole input fits in its buffer, so on Unix `buffered_stdin` now writes the input into a fresh pipe with a nonblocking writer before spawn and closes the writer. Only input larger than the pipe buffer (64 KiB on macOS and Linux) falls back to the temp file, and that case still needs a usable `TMPDIR`. Windows keeps the temp file.

Verified with the release-review repros: with `TMPDIR=/nonexistent/dir`, the post-start hook runs, `for-each` succeeds, `wt list` shows the dirty worktree, and `wt remove` exits 0, matching v0.80.0. The existing list TMPDIR test now adds an untracked file and requires empty stderr, and a new remove test covers the detached cleanup; both fail without the fix. The existing `test_cmd_with_stdin` covers empty input and a 1.7 MB input that takes the temp-file path.

title: fix(copy-ignored): give copied files their source's mtime
body:
Since v0.80.0, `wt step copy-ignored` produces stale cargo builds. #4319 stamps every copied file with one time taken after `git worktree add`, so a copied `target/` looks newer than the sources that checkout just wrote, and cargo treats it as up to date. Repro: build v1 in main, commit v2 without rebuilding, `wt switch --create feat`, `wt step copy-ignored`, `cargo build`. On main cargo finishes in 0.00s and the binary prints v1; v0.80.0 (which kept source mtimes through clonefile on macOS) recompiles and prints v2.

This gives each copied regular file its source's mtime, as `cp -a` does, on every platform, and removes the stamp parameter. That still covers #4248's Linux case, where parallel copies ordered files by scheduling: #4319's own table shows `cp -a` recompiles the same two units as the stamp. `wt step promote`'s cross-device fallback shares the helper, so it now keeps mtimes too, like `mv` across filesystems. Symlinks and directories keep the copy time, as in v0.80.0.

Verified on macOS: the repro above now recompiles and prints v2, and a tree with 2020-dated ignored files keeps the same mtimes as v0.80.0. The new integration test copies files with distinct past mtimes through a directory entry and a top-level entry; it fails on main and passes here. The read-only unit test now asserts the source mtime.

Not covered, on v0.80.0 either: copying into an existing worktree whose sources were checked out before the source worktree's build still leaves outputs newer than those sources, so cargo reuses them.

title: fix(remove): drain the trash with one background process per repository
body:
A prune of many worktrees started one `rm -rf` per staged worktree. On a 193-worktree prune those processes competed for the disk: together they deleted about 1,500 files/s on 3 cores, while a single `rm` alone managed 3,000–5,400 files/s on under one core. Read-only directories (`dr-xr-xr-x`, as installers leave them) also made `rm -rf` fail, so those entries stayed in `.git/wt/trash/` and every later sweep retried them.

Removal now starts a hidden `wt _drain-trash`, which holds `.git/wt/trash.lock` and deletes every staged entry, including entries staged while it runs. A removal or sweep that finds the lock held starts nothing, so a prune runs about one deleter. The sweep after `wt remove` drains leftovers immediately rather than waiting 24 hours. Priority is unchanged (`taskpolicy -b` on macOS).

The drain uses wt's own walker (`src/remove_dir.rs`), which `wt remove --foreground` and `wt config state clear` also use:

- On Unix it opens each directory relative to its parent's descriptor with `O_NOFOLLOW` and unlinks relative to the holding directory. The old path-based walker could follow a directory swapped for a symlink mid-walk and delete outside the tree; a swap-race script reproduced that, and the new walker lost nothing in 20 runs.
- It grants the owner `rwx` on each directory it enters, so read-only and unreadable trees are deleted, never changing a symlink's target. Linux's `fchmodat` has no `AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW`, so there it opens the directory with `O_PATH | O_NOFOLLOW` and changes the mode through `/proc/self/fd`.
- Subdirectories are removed sequentially, so open descriptors stay bounded by depth. On a 199k-entry pnpm `node_modules` it deleted about twice as fast as `rm -rf`.
- On Windows it uses `std::fs::remove_dir_all`, which removes junctions without following them.
